text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, basic cattle care centers on adequate forage/feed (grasses, hay, crop residues), clean water, shelter or shade, and daily observation. Cattle are ruminants, so their diet should contain substantial fibrous feed, with additional energy, protein, minerals, and vitamins when available forage does not meet needs. Quality and quantity of forage changes considerably between wet season (roughly May–October, when pasture is more abundant but heavy rain, mud, and flooding can reduce grazing access and contaminate feed) and dry season (roughly November–April, when forage availability declines, so farmers should conserve suitable feed ahead of time rather than waiting until animals lose condition). Clean water should be available regularly, with particular attention during hot weather. Farmers should observe appetite, rumination, manure, body condition, movement, breathing, coat, and unusual behavior daily. Sudden large diet changes, especially concentrated/fermentable feed, should be avoided; feed changes should be gradual. Moldy, rotten, or chemically contaminated feed should never be given. Cattle should have shade and protection from heat, rain, and mud. Do not assume irrigated pasture, purchased compound feed, or specialized housing — start with locally available safe forage and crop residues, and base mineral/concentrate supplementation on the animal's actual condition and local veterinary advice, not a generic recommendation. Cambodia has several cattle types (Kouprey-influenced indigenous cattle, local yellow cattle, Brahman-influenced/improved cattle), but there is not enough province-specific evidence to name one as predominant in Preah Vihear — ask the farmer what type they keep rather than guessing from location. Practical progression: adequate local forage → clean water → shade → safe feed storage → daily observation → seasonal feed planning → veterinary support when needed.
